text: They marked the victory properly that evening, the whole camp gathered around a fire built larger than strictly necessary, Brother Crumb producing a spread that suggested he'd been quietly saving provisions for exactly this occasion, Will already three stories deep into an account of his own battlefield heroics that grew more improbable with each retelling.
“I distinctly recall holding that flank alone against considerably worse odds than you're describing,” Long John said, mild, watching Will's story expand with real, long-suffering affection.
“Artistic embellishment,” Will said, entirely unrepentant. “The essential truth remains intact. I was, at minimum, present and reasonably heroic.”

Pip sat close beside Thistlewood, both of them quiet in the particular contented way of people who'd spent the whole day braced for considerably worse than what had actually happened, watching the gathered warmth with something like disbelief still lingering beneath their evident relief.
“We won,” Pip said, simply, testing the words.

“We did,” Thistlewood agreed. “Rather more thoroughly than I'd allowed myself to properly hope for, if I'm honest about where my expectations sat this morning.” He looked around at the whole assembled family — blood and chosen, old and new, all of it thoroughly, permanently entangled now — and found himself smiling in a way that felt, after so many years of careful caution, genuinely unguarded.

sequence._describe: Robin of Loxby sitting beside his father Edmund a little apart from the gathering, a quiet meaningful conversation by the firelight. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. Wide shot, 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, warm intimate evening firelight, tender contemplative mood.

text: It was Robin who found his father sitting a little apart from the main gathering, watching the fire with the particular quiet stillness of a man turning over a decision he hadn't quite finished making.
“You're thinking about going home,” Robin said, settling beside him.

“I was,” Edmund admitted. “There's still a household to properly manage, whatever's left of it. A steward who's earned rather more loyalty than I've ever properly repaid him for.” He paused, something considering working behind his weathered features. “But I find, sitting here tonight, that I'm no longer entirely certain 'home' means the same place it did a week ago.”
“It doesn't have to,” Robin said, quiet. “Not if you'd rather it meant something else instead.”

“I spent years believing distance was the safest thing I could offer the people I loved,” Edmund said, echoing his own words from days before with real, settled conviction behind them now. “I find I've had rather enough of that particular belief, having watched today exactly what closeness properly defended actually looks like.” He turned to face Robin directly. “I'd like to stay. Not forever, necessarily — I'll need to see to the household eventually, make certain the steward's looked after properly. But for now, if you'll have me, I find I'd rather learn what it means to be your father properly, in person, rather than through distant arrangements and careful debts.”
“I'd like that,” Robin said, something warm and unguarded working plainly across his features. “I've only just gotten you back. I'm not in any particular hurry to lose you to distance again.”

text: The days that followed settled into something Robin found himself treasuring in ways he hadn't properly anticipated — Edmund slowly, awkwardly, joyfully integrating into the camp's established rhythms, learning the cant with the same delighted confusion he'd shown that first evening, losing to Will at cards with a regularity that suggested either genuine incompetence or considerable paternal patience.

“Your father,” Marian observed, watching Edmund lose spectacularly to Will for what seemed the fourth consecutive round, “is either remarkably bad at cards, or remarkably good at letting Will believe he's remarkably good at cards.”
“Knowing him now,” Robin said, “I genuinely couldn't tell you which.”

Robin found his own aim no more improved than it had ever been, though he noticed, practicing one crisp morning with his father watching nearby, that he minded the poor accuracy considerably less than he once had — some old anxious need to prove himself having quietly, gently loosened its grip somewhere across this long, improbable year.
“Your grandfather would be proud,” Edmund said, watching another arrow sail wide. “Not of the aim. Simply of the man doing the missing.”

Marian, watching from a short distance with Grimalkin curled at her feet, allowed herself a small, private smile at the sight of them both — father and son, finally, properly, learning each other, one imperfect arrow at a time.

sequence._describe: Robin of Loxby and Marian Fletcher sitting together at the fire's edge in the evening, holding hands, a quiet reflective conversation about the journey and what remains ahead. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. Wide shot, 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, soft warm evening firelight, tender reflective mood.

text: That evening, once the camp had settled into its familiar quiet warmth, Marian found Robin at the fire's edge, watching the flames with the particular contemplative stillness she'd come to recognize as him properly turning something over.
“We've come rather a long way,” he said, when she settled beside him, “from a man who couldn't hit a target if his life depended on it, terrified of a Sheriff he'd never even properly met.”

“You've come further than that,” Marian said. “You know the whole truth now — about Thistlewood, about Pip, about your father, about yourself. That's not nothing, Robin. That's rather everything, if you think about it properly.”
“It doesn't feel finished, though,” Robin said, quiet. “Whatever we've won here. The Sheriff's still out there. Whatever comes next, I don't think we've seen the last of him.”

“No,” Marian agreed, honest even now, in this hard-won moment of peace. “We haven't. But we face whatever comes next as exactly who we are now — a family, whole and honest, with nothing left hidden between us that matters.” She took his hand, steady, warm, entirely certain. “That's worth considerably more than false comfort, Robin. Whatever the Sheriff brings, whenever he finally brings it, we'll face it together, same as we've faced everything else this past remarkable year.”

Robin looked at her, at the fire, at the whole assembled family settling into contented sleep around them, and found, despite the uncertainty still waiting somewhere beyond tonight's fragile peace, that he felt something close to genuine hope.
“Together,” he agreed. “Whatever comes.”

Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. text: Some considerable distance away, in a cold stone hall that had never once needed banners or gilding to make its particular point, the Sheriff of Nottingham received the news of his Captain's failure with the same unhurried, unsettling calm that had defined every other moment of his long, careful career.

“She stood down,” the messenger reported, visibly uneasy delivering the account. “Ordered her own retreat, mid-battle, with the objective very nearly in hand. Word is she means to resign her commission entirely, rather than explain herself to you directly.”
The Sheriff was quiet a long moment, turning the report over with the particular patient attention he brought to anything that genuinely mattered, before finally, deliberately, setting it aside.

“Captain Blackwood,” he said, at last, something cold and considering beneath his usual composed calm, “was, I confess, rather better than I properly gave her credit for — competent enough to nearly succeed, and apparently possessed of scruples I hadn't accounted for in my own calculations. I shall need to remember that particular lesson, going forward.”
He rose, moving to the window, looking out over Nottingham's cobbled streets with the same patient, unhurried attention he gave everything else.

“An old debt, a reunited family, a Captain who discovered a conscience at precisely the worst possible moment,” he said, quiet, almost to himself. “I find I've learned rather a great deal today about exactly what I'm dealing with.” He turned back toward the room, something final and entirely resolved settling into his composed features. “It seems, if this matter is to be properly resolved at last, I shall simply have to attend to it myself. Whatever peace they believe they've won today, in Sherwood — it was never going to be the ending. Merely a very brief, very costly delay.”
Outside, Nottingham's evening bells began their familiar toll, indifferent as ever to the quiet, patient promise of a reckoning not yet finished — only, for now, postponed.
